original.basis: Class-default 15-30% band ('class default band, no part-specific estimate made') applied to an affected cost of £181.62 = cell £122.41 + BMS £40.00 + housing £19.21, as if de-bundling saved a share of the parts' own price. Risk-adjusted £19.07-£38.14 at p 0.7, NRE £50,000, payback 0.02 yr (Evaluation, ID-138).

corrected.basis: De-bundling removes margin, not part cost, so the ceiling is the margin the study's own cascade puts on the content being moved. Summary_Assembly charges SG&A at 6% on supplier cost minus the cell (£259.33 - £122.41 = £136.91, giving £8.21). It charges profit at 6% on that base plus SG&A (£8.71), which is margin-on-margin. The cell carries no SG&A or profit, only a 1.5% handling charge (£1.84), because EVE makes both the cells and the pack and the cell price already includes the cell maker's margin. The total removable pool is therefore £18.76, not £27-£54. The idea moves the BMS (£40.00) and the housing (£19.21) out of the assembler's marked-up base. The margin on that £59.21 is £59.21 x (1.06 x 1.06 - 1) = £7.32. The rest of the bought-in parts and the assembly conversion stay with whoever assembles the pack and keep their margin. The low case assumes the assembler still charges the study's own 1.5% handling rate on directed BMS and housing (-£0.89) and that cell handling stays. The high case assumes the cell handling charge is also removed (+£1.84). Both cases then deduct the OEM's added purchasing cost on the £181.62 now contracted directly: 1.2% of spend (CAPS industrial-manufacturing average) in the low case and 0.59% (Hackett world class) in the high case, i.e. £2.18 / £1.07. The result is £4.25-£8.08/pack, within the £18.76 margin pool. Not booked: in-house integration engineering, the functional safety case, incoming quality and the warranty liability that moves to the OEM under a directed-buy arrangement have no cited public percentage and are not deducted. Together they could plausibly absorb the remainder. The figure is a ceiling to test with the idea's own validation step (turnkey quote against direct content plus integration cost).

systemTradeNote: ID-138 currently wins C20 over ID-013 (dual-source the cell, risk-adjusted £3.43-£7.71) and C36 over ID-058 (BMS retender, deep-dive part-specific, £4.20-£8.40). Corrected, ID-138 at £2.98-£5.66 is below ID-058, and both ID-013 and ID-058 score higher on weighted score (4.80 and 4.47 against 3.93), so re-run the conflict graph. ID-058 attacks the BMS price directly and probably captures more than de-bundling its margin. De-bundling also moves warranty, the functional safety case and pack performance guarantees from EVE to the OEM. The study's warranty provision (£3.34, 1.2%) and the single-supplier performance guarantee are system-level costs this idea shifts rather than removes.

research.claim: Supplier margins around 6% (the study's profit rate) are realistic
research.finding: Roland Berger/Lazard Global Automotive Supplier Study 2025: average supplier EBIT 4.7% in 2024 (5.3% in 2023); Chinese suppliers highest at 5.7%. The study's 6% is at or slightly above the benchmark, so the margin pool is if anything generous.

research.claim: OEM purchasing cost as a share of spend
research.finding: ISM citing Hackett (2016): average 0.72%, world class 0.59% of spend. CAPS Research (2014): industrial manufacturing 1.2%, overall average 1.2%. Dated, and covers purchasing only, not integration, quality or warranty.

research.claim: OEMs commonly source cells directly and use a third party for the rest (system integration model)
research.finding: S&P Global Mobility: the 'system integration' model, where the OEM manages supply of one or two components and a third party sources the rest, covers about 54% of battery GWh. The model is real, but no margin saving is quantified.

research.claim: Published tier-1 handling fee / markup on OEM-directed (directed-buy) parts
research.finding: No public figure found. An FGV paper on directed-buy agreements covers tier-1 liability limits for warranty and line stoppage on OEM-imposed tier-2s, which supports the point that liability moves to the OEM, but gives no fee.

research.claim: Consultancy (McKinsey/BCG/Bain/PwC) benchmark for margin stacking on bought-in cells in turnkey battery supply
research.finding: None found in the searches run. Roland Berger's battery-strategy piece discusses OEM dependency on cell makers but gives no margin-stack figure.
The National Academies figure covers vehicle-level indirect costs (OEM RPE), not tier-1 margin on bought-in content. Not used.

summary: The £27-£54/pack claim exceeded the entire margin layer in the study's own cost build-up, which is £18.76: SG&A £8.21 + profit £8.71 + cell handling £1.84. The cells carry no pack-supplier margin because EVE makes both. Removing the margin on the directly sourced BMS and housing, net of the OEM's added purchasing cost, gives at most £4.25-£8.08/pack (£2.98-£5.66 risk-adjusted), before integration, safety-case and warranty costs that move in-house. Treat it as a ceiling to be tested by quotation, not a booked saving, and re-run the conflict with the BMS retender (ID-058), which now looks the stronger idea.
